claim: Oct4 is essential for the maintenance and induction of stem cell pluripotency.
source: The transcription factor Oct4 is essential for the maintenance and induction of stem cell pluripotency, but its functional roles are not fully understood.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Niwa et al., 2000; Nichols et al., 1998).

claim: Oct4 depletion leads to an immediate loss of its binding to enhancers.
source: Oct4 depletion leads to an immediate loss of its binding to enhancers, accompanied by a decrease in mRNA synthesis from its target genes that are part of the transcriptional network that maintains pluripotency.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data showing Oct4 occupancy decreased after 3 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 1A, chromatin; Figure 4E).

claim: Oct4 depletion leads to a decrease in mRNA synthesis from its target genes that are part of the transcriptional network that maintains pluripotency.
source: Oct4 depletion leads to an immediate loss of its binding to enhancers, accompanied by a decrease in mRNA synthesis from its target genes that are part of the transcriptional network that maintains pluripotency.
evidence: This is supported by TT-seq data showing changes in mRNA synthesis after 3 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Gradual decrease of Oct4 binding to enhancers does not immediately change the chromatin accessibility.
source: Gradual decrease of Oct4 binding to enhancers does not immediately change the chromatin accessibility but reduces transcription of enhancers.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data showing chromatin accessibility remained largely unchanged at 3 hr (Figure 5B).

claim: Gradual decrease of Oct4 binding to enhancers reduces transcription of enhancers.
source: Gradual decrease of Oct4 binding to enhancers does not immediately change the chromatin accessibility but reduces transcription of enhancers.
evidence: This is supported by TT-seq data showing eRNA synthesis decreased rapidly at Oct4-bound enhancers (Figure 4B).

claim: Partial recovery of Oct4 expression results in a rapid increase in chromatin accessibility.
source: Conversely, partial recovery of Oct4 expression results in a rapid increase in chromatin accessibility, whereas enhancer transcription does not fully recover.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data showing a strong increase of chromatin accessibility after 4.5 hr of DOX washout (Figure 8C).

claim: Partial recovery of Oct4 expression does not lead to full recovery of enhancer transcription.
source: Conversely, partial recovery of Oct4 expression results in a rapid increase in chromatin accessibility, whereas enhancer transcription does not fully recover.
evidence: This is supported by TT-seq data showing weak but significant upregulation of eRNA synthesis at Oct4-sensitive enhancers (Figure 8C).

claim: Normal ESC levels of Oct4 are required for transcription of pluripotency enhancers.
source: Whereas normal ESC levels of Oct4 are required for transcription of pluripotency enhancers, low levels of Oct4 are sufficient to retain chromatin accessibility, likely together with other factors such as Sox2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eRNA synthesis decreased rapidly at Oct4-bound enhancers during depletion (Figure 4B) and could not be fully recovered during partial recovery (Figure 8C).

claim: Low levels of Oct4 are sufficient to retain chromatin accessibility.
source: Whereas normal ESC levels of Oct4 are required for transcription of pluripotency enhancers, low levels of Oct4 are sufficient to retain chromatin accessibility, likely together with other factors such as Sox2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromatin accessibility was largely restored during partial recovery when Oct4 levels were still low (Figure 8C).

claim: Oct4 is essential for maintaining pluripotency in vitro.
source: The transcription factor (TF) Oct4 is essential for maintaining pluripotency in vitro (Niwa et al., 2000) as well as in vivo (Nichols et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2000.

claim: Oct4 is essential for maintaining pluripotency in vivo.
source: The transcription factor (TF) Oct4 is essential for maintaining pluripotency in vitro (Niwa et al., 2000) as well as in vivo (Nichols et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nichols et al., 1998.

claim: Oct4 lies at the core of an intricate transcriptional regulatory network that maintains the pluripotent state.
source: Oct4 lies at the core of an intricate transcriptional regulatory network that maintains the pluripotent state (Boyer et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007) and Oct4-driven protein–protein interactions are crucial for maintaining and inducing pluripotency (Esch et al., 2013; Han et al., 2022; van den Berg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boyer et al., 2005 and Zhou et al., 2007.

claim: Oct4-driven protein–protein interactions are crucial for maintaining and inducing pluripotency.
source: Oct4 lies at the core of an intricate transcriptional regulatory network that maintains the pluripotent state (Boyer et al., 2005; Zhou et al., 2007) and Oct4-driven protein–protein interactions are crucial for maintaining and inducing pluripotency (Esch et al., 2013; Han et al., 2022; van den Berg et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esch et al., 2013; Han et al., 2022; van den Berg et al., 2010.

claim: Oct4 knockout in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) leads to a quick disruption of the pluripotency state and differentiation of the ESCs into trophectoderm.
source: Oct4 knockout in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) leads to a quick disruption of the pluripotency state and differentiation of the ESCs into trophectoderm (Niwa et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2000.

claim: Oct4 binds to enhancers.
source: Oct4 binds to enhancers (Schöler et al., 1989), which are cis-regulatory genomic elements that orchestrate gene expression in metazoans (Banerji et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schöler et al., 1989.

claim: Enhancers are cis-regulatory genomic elements that orchestrate gene expression in metazoans.
source: Oct4 binds to enhancers (Schöler et al., 1989), which are cis-regulatory genomic elements that orchestrate gene expression in metazoans (Banerji et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Banerji et al., 1981.

claim: Oct4 function in maintaining pluripotency of ESCs has been attributed to the establishment of superenhancers (SEs).
source: Oct4 function in maintaining pluripotency of ESCs has been attributed to the establishment of superenhancers (SEs), that have high occupancy of TFs and coactivators (Hnisz et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hnisz et al., 2013 and Whyte et al., 2013.

claim: Superenhancers have high occupancy of TFs and coactivators.
source: Oct4 function in maintaining pluripotency of ESCs has been attributed to the establishment of superenhancers (SEs), that have high occupancy of TFs and coactivators (Hnisz et al., 2013; Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hnisz et al., 2013 and Whyte et al., 2013.

claim: Degradation of Oct4 leads to preferential decrease of Oct4 and Mediator occupancy at SEs.
source: Degradation of Oct4 leads to preferential decrease of Oct4 and Mediator occupancy at SEs (Boija et al., 2018) and consequent downregulation of pluripotency genes that are located near SEs (Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boija et al., 2018.

claim: Degradation of Oct4 leads to consequent downregulation of pluripotency genes that are located near SEs.
source: Degradation of Oct4 leads to preferential decrease of Oct4 and Mediator occupancy at SEs (Boija et al., 2018) and consequent downregulation of pluripotency genes that are located near SEs (Whyte et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Whyte et al., 2013.

claim: Oct4 cooperates with the TF Sox2 at thousands of genomic sites in ESCs.
source: Oct4 cooperates with the TF Sox2 at thousands of genomic sites in ESCs (Ambrosetti et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2008; Loh et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ambrosetti et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2008; Loh et al., 2006; Yuan et al., 1995.

claim: Oct4 and Sox2 cooperatively bind the SoxOct composite motif present in their target enhancers.
source: Oct4 and Sox2 cooperatively bind the SoxOct composite motif present in their target enhancers (Chen et al., 2008; Lam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2008 and Lam et al., 2012.

claim: Prolonged depletion of Oct4 for 24 hr in ESCs resulted in a loss of chromatin accessibility at the majority of its occupied sites.
source: A previous study showed that prolonged depletion of Oct4 for 24 hr in ESCs resulted in a loss of chromatin accessibility at the majority of its occupied sites, accompanied by a loss of Sox2 binding (King and Klose, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King and Klose, 2017.

claim: Prolonged depletion of Oct4 for 24 hr in ESCs was accompanied by a loss of Sox2 binding.
source: A previous study showed that prolonged depletion of Oct4 for 24 hr in ESCs resulted in a loss of chromatin accessibility at the majority of its occupied sites, accompanied by a loss of Sox2 binding (King and Klose, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King and Klose, 2017.

claim: Chromatin accessibility is regulated in a highly dynamic manner with Oct4 being constantly required.
source: Using an Oct4 protein depletion system in ESCs, another study suggested that chromatin accessibility is regulated in a highly dynamic manner with Oct4 being constantly required (Friman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Friman et al., 2019.

claim: Enhancers are often transcribed resulting in the production of enhancer RNAs (eRNAs).
source: Enhancers are often transcribed resulting in the production of enhancer RNAs (eRNAs) (De Santa et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2010; Tuan et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to De Santa et al., 2010; Kim et al., 2010; Tuan et al., 1992.

claim: Transcribing Pol II at enhancers contributes to chromatin alterations by recruiting histone modifying and remodeling factors.
source: Transcribing Pol II at enhancers contributes to chromatin alterations by recruiting histone modifying and remodeling factors (Ho et al., 2006; Kaikkonen et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2004), and eRNA may be involved in gene regulation (Bose et al., 2017; Gorbovytska et al., 2021; Kaikkonen et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Mousavi et al., 2013; Schaukowitch et al., 2014; Sigova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ho et al., 2006; Kaikkonen et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2004.

claim: eRNA may be involved in gene regulation.
source: Transcribing Pol II at enhancers contributes to chromatin alterations by recruiting histone modifying and remodeling factors (Ho et al., 2006; Kaikkonen et al., 2013; Ling et al., 2004), and eRNA may be involved in gene regulation (Bose et al., 2017; Gorbovytska et al., 2021; Kaikkonen et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Mousavi et al., 2013; Schaukowitch et al., 2014; Sigova et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bose et al., 2017; Gorbovytska et al., 2021; Kaikkonen et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013; Mousavi et al., 2013; Schaukowitch et al., 2014; Sigova et al., 2015.

claim: The synthesis of eRNA correlates with the transactivation activity of enhancers.
source: The synthesis of eRNA correlates with the transactivation activity of enhancers (Andersson et al., 2014; De Santa et al., 2010; Djebali et al., 2012; Hah et al., 2013; Henriques et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2010; Melgar et al., 2011; Michel et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andersson et al., 2014; De Santa et al., 2010; Djebali et al., 2012; Hah et al., 2013; Henriques et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2010; Melgar et al., 2011; Michel et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2014.

claim: The synthesis of eRNA can be used to identify putative enhancers by transient transcriptome sequencing (TT-seq).
source: The synthesis of eRNA can be used to identify putative enhancers by transient transcriptome sequencing (TT-seq), a method that captures newly synthesized RNA (Schwalb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwalb et al., 2016.

claim: TT-seq is a method that captures newly synthesized RNA.
source: The synthesis of eRNA can be used to identify putative enhancers by transient transcriptome sequencing (TT-seq), a method that captures newly synthesized RNA (Schwalb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwalb et al., 2016.

claim: TT-seq combines a short pulse of 4-thiouridine (4sU) labeling with RNA fragmentation and monitors transcription changes at both enhancers and their target genes genome-wide.
source: TT-seq combines a short pulse of 4-thiouridine (4sU) labeling with RNA fragmentation and monitors transcription changes at both enhancers and their target genes genome-wide (Schwalb et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwalb et al., 2016.

claim: TT-seq can quantify changes in enhancer transcription and is ideal to monitor immediate transcriptome changes after perturbation.
source: TT-seq can quantify changes in enhancer transcription and is ideal to monitor immediate transcriptome changes after perturbation (Choi et al., 2021; Gressel et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2021; Gressel et al., 2019; Michel et al., 2017.

claim: Oct4 protein levels were already reduced after 6 hr of DOX treatment and substantially decreased after 9 hr.
source: We found that Oct4 protein levels were already reduced after 6 hr of treatment and substantially decreased after 9 hr (Figure 1A, whole cell lysate).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Oct4 protein depletion was complete at 24 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Oct4 protein depletion was complete at 24 hr of treatment, while Sox2 and Nanog protein levels remained mostly unchanged for extended times before eventually decreasing (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sox2 and Nanog protein levels remained mostly unchanged for extended times before eventually decreasing during Oct4 depletion.
source: Oct4 protein depletion was complete at 24 hr of treatment, while Sox2 and Nanog protein levels remained mostly unchanged for extended times before eventually decreasing (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chromatin binding of Oct4 was reduced already after 3 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Chromatin binding of Oct4 was reduced already after 3 hr of DOX treatment, whereas Sox2 binding decreased after 9 hr and Nanog binding remained unchanged over the entire time course (Figure 1A, chromatin).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data of chromatin fractions shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Sox2 chromatin binding decreased after 9 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Chromatin binding of Oct4 was reduced already after 3 hr of DOX treatment, whereas Sox2 binding decreased after 9 hr and Nanog binding remained unchanged over the entire time course (Figure 1A, chromatin).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data of chromatin fractions shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nanog chromatin binding remained unchanged over the entire time course of Oct4 depletion.
source: Chromatin binding of Oct4 was reduced already after 3 hr of DOX treatment, whereas Sox2 binding decreased after 9 hr and Nanog binding remained unchanged over the entire time course (Figure 1A, chromatin).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data of chromatin fractions shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the chromatin fraction Oct4 levels gradually decreased to 87.5% (3 hr), 50.5% (6 hr), 17.0% (9 hr), 7.0% (12 hr), and 2.5% (15 hr) compared to 0 hr.
source: In the chromatin fraction Oct4 levels gradually decreased to 87.5% (3 hr), 50.5% (6 hr), 17.0% (9 hr), 7.0% (12 hr), and 2.5% (15 hr), whereas Sox2 levels slightly increased to 126.8% (3 hr) and 112.5% (6 hr), and then decreased to 32.4% (9 hr), 16.4% (12 hr), and 1.7% (15 hr) compared to 0 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Sox2 levels in the chromatin fraction slightly increased to 126.8% (3 hr) and 112.5% (6 hr), and then decreased to 32.4% (9 hr), 16.4% (12 hr), and 1.7% (15 hr) compared to 0 hr.
source: In the chromatin fraction Oct4 levels gradually decreased to 87.5% (3 hr), 50.5% (6 hr), 17.0% (9 hr), 7.0% (12 hr), and 2.5% (15 hr), whereas Sox2 levels slightly increased to 126.8% (3 hr) and 112.5% (6 hr), and then decreased to 32.4% (9 hr), 16.4% (12 hr), and 1.7% (15 hr) compared to 0 hr.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Changes in mRNA synthesis could already be observed after 3 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Changes could already be observed after 3 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), in agreement with chromatin fractionation results (Figure 1A, chromatin).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis of TT-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis detected 769 significantly downregulated and 829 upregulated genes after 15 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Differential gene expression analysis (Love et al., 2014) detected 769 significantly downregulated and 829 upregulated genes (adjusted p value <0.01) after 15 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 2A, B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by DESeq2 analysis of TT-seq data shown in Figure 2A, B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Early downregulated genes (446 genes) showed the strongest decrease in mRNA synthesis after 6–9 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Early downregulated genes (446 genes) showed the strongest decrease in mRNA synthesis after 6–9 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 2C, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, left), whereas late downregulated genes (323 genes) decreased most strongly after 12–15 hr (Figure 2C, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, right).
evidence: This is supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C, D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Late downregulated genes (323 genes) decreased most strongly after 12–15 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Early downregulated genes (446 genes) showed the strongest decrease in mRNA synthesis after 6–9 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 2C, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, left), whereas late downregulated genes (323 genes) decreased most strongly after 12–15 hr (Figure 2C, D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, right).
evidence: This is supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 2C, D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Early downregulated genes were enriched for stem cell population maintenance.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis (Huang et al., 2009) showed that early downregulated genes were enriched for stem cell population maintenance (Figure 2E), whereas late downregulated genes were enriched for DNA replication and cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Late downregulated genes were enriched for DNA replication and cell cycle.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis (Huang et al., 2009) showed that early downregulated genes were enriched for stem cell population maintenance (Figure 2E), whereas late downregulated genes were enriched for DNA replication and cell cycle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Early upregulated genes showed enrichment for carbohydrate metabolic processes.
source: Early upregulated genes showed enrichment for carbohydrate metabolic processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), and late upregulated genes were enriched for in utero embryonic development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Late upregulated genes were enriched for in utero embryonic development.
source: Early upregulated genes showed enrichment for carbohydrate metabolic processes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H), and late upregulated genes were enriched for in utero embryonic development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Of the 150 transcribed genes that are nearest to SEs, 60 were significantly downregulated, of which 45 were early downregulated.
source: Indeed, of the 150 transcribed genes that are nearest to SEs (Whyte et al., 2013), 60 were significantly downregulated, of which 45 were early downregulated (Figure 2F, p value = 2.6e−24, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SE-controlled genes shown in Figure 2F.

claim: mRNA synthesis of SE-controlled downregulated genes was particularly sensitive to Oct4 depletion.
source: We then compared the kinetics of mRNA synthesis changes of the putatively SE-controlled downregulated genes (60) to other downregulated genes (709). mRNA synthesis of SE-controlled downregulated genes was particularly sensitive to Oct4 depletion (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of mRNA synthesis kinetics shown in Figure 2G.

claim: At 6 hr of Oct4 depletion there was a significant downregulation of Esrrb, Klf2, Klf4, Utf1, and Tbx3.
source: At 6 hr of Oct4 depletion we found a significant downregulation of Esrrb, Klf2, Klf4, Utf1, and Tbx3. At 9 hr of depletion, Sox2, Nanog, and Prdm14 were significantly downregulated, and Nr5a2 and Fgf4 after 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: At 9 hr of Oct4 depletion, Sox2, Nanog, and Prdm14 were significantly downregulated.
source: At 6 hr of Oct4 depletion we found a significant downregulation of Esrrb, Klf2, Klf4, Utf1, and Tbx3. At 9 hr of depletion, Sox2, Nanog, and Prdm14 were significantly downregulated, and Nr5a2 and Fgf4 after 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: At 12 hr of Oct4 depletion, Nr5a2 and Fgf4 were significantly downregulated.
source: At 6 hr of Oct4 depletion we found a significant downregulation of Esrrb, Klf2, Klf4, Utf1, and Tbx3. At 9 hr of depletion, Sox2, Nanog, and Prdm14 were significantly downregulated, and Nr5a2 and Fgf4 after 12 hr.
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Oct4 is required to maintain the transcriptional network underlying pluripotency.
source: Taken together, our analysis of early mRNA synthesis changes upon Oct4 depletion revealed a rapid downregulation of the components of the pluripotency transcriptional network with SE-controlled genes being immediately and strongly affected. Thus, consistent with previous findings (Whyte et al., 2013), Oct4 is required to maintain the transcriptional network underlying pluripotency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early downregulated genes were enriched for stem cell population maintenance and SE-controlled genes were particularly sensitive to Oct4 depletion.

claim: The majority of Oct4 ChIP-seq peaks (91%) overlapped with open chromatin regions identified by ATAC-seq.
source: Most Oct4 ChIP-seq peaks (91%) overlapped with open chromatin regions identified by ATAC-seq (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Out of the 8727 putative eRNAs, 2221 overlapped with 2231 Oct4-bound sites.
source: Out of the 8727 putative eRNAs, 2221 overlapped with 2231 Oct4-bound sites (Klf4 SE shown as an example in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis and genome browser view shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The majority of Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers (90%) were marked by histone H3 lysine 4 mono-methylation (H3K4me1).
source: The majority of Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers (90%) were marked by histone H3 lysine 4 mono-methylation (H3K4me1) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers were strongly enriched for biological processes related to stem cell population maintenance.
source: Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers were strongly enriched for biological processes related to stem cell population maintenance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: eRNAs originating from Oct4-bound enhancers were significantly longer and showed higher synthesis than other eRNAs.
source: eRNAs originating from Oct4-bound enhancers were significantly longer and showed higher synthesis than other eRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, p value <2.2e−16, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is supported by comparison analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers were enriched with active histone marks H3K27ac and H3K4me3, higher chromatin accessibility, and higher occupancies of Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4, and Esrrb compared to Oct4-bound nontranscribed enhancers.
source: Whereas both groups of enhancers showed similar H3K4me1 levels, Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers were enriched with active histone marks H3K27ac and H3K4me3, higher chromatin accessibility, and higher occupancies of Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4, and Esrrb (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers were located closer to their nearest active putative target genes (median distance of 37 kb) as compared to nontranscribed enhancers (median distance 89 kb).
source: Moreover, Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers were located closer to their nearest active putative target genes (median distance of 37 kb) as compared to nontranscribed enhancers (median distance 89 kb) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by distance distribution analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Half of the Oct4-bound sites within SEs produced eRNAs.
source: Finally, we investigated eRNA synthesis at SEs. Half of the Oct4-bound sites within SEs produced eRNAs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by pie chart analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The eRNAs obtained from SEs were generally longer and had higher synthesis levels compared to eRNAs from typical enhancers (TEs).
source: The eRNAs obtained from SEs were generally longer and had higher synthesis levels compared to eRNAs from typical enhancers (TEs), and SEs showed higher occupancy with Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4, and Esrrb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, K).
evidence: This is supported by comparison analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, K.

claim: SEs showed higher occupancy with Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4, and Esrrb compared to typical enhancers.
source: The eRNAs obtained from SEs were generally longer and had higher synthesis levels compared to eRNAs from typical enhancers (TEs), and SEs showed higher occupancy with Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4, and Esrrb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, K).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J, K.

claim: Differential expression analysis of eRNAs detected significant downregulation of 782 Oct4-regulated eRNAs after 15 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Differential expression analysis of eRNAs (Love et al., 2014) detected significant downregulation of 782 Oct4-regulated eRNAs after 15 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, adjusted p value <0.01).
evidence: This is supported by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: For the downregulated eRNAs synthesis decreased already after 3 hr of DOX treatment.
source: The kinetics analysis showed that for the downregulated eRNAs synthesis decreased already after 3 hr (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SE eRNAs were more strongly downregulated compared to TE eRNAs.
source: Moreover, SE eRNAs were more strongly downregulated compared to TE eRNAs (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison analysis shown in Figure 4C, D.

claim: Compared to Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers, the proportion of downregulated eRNAs was ~fivefold lower for Oct4-unbound transcribed enhancers.
source: Compared to Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers, the proportion of downregulated eRNAs was ~fivefold lower for Oct4-unbound transcribed enhancers, and their eRNA synthesis changes were generally observed later, likely representing secondary effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Oct4 is required for eRNA synthesis at about one third of putative Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers including SEs.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Oct4 is required for eRNA synthesis at about one third of putative Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers including SEs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 782 out of 2221 Oct4-regulated eRNAs were significantly downregulated.

claim: Oct4 occupancy decreased over the time course of DOX treatment at downregulated eRNAs.
source: In agreement with chromatin fractionation results (Figure 1A, chromatin), Oct4 occupancy decreased after 3 hr and strongly dropped after 9 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Occupancy of Oct4 decreased more strongly at SEs compared to TEs.
source: In accordance with our previous results (Figure 4D), occupancy of Oct4 decreased more strongly at SEs compared to TEs (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Oct4 binding is required for eRNA synthesis at a subset of Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers and particularly at SEs.
source: These results show that Oct4 binding is required for eRNA synthesis at a subset of Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers and particularly at SEs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Oct4 occupancy decreased and eRNA synthesis decreased at downregulated eRNAs, with stronger effects at SEs.

claim: About half of SE-nearest genes showed downregulated mRNA synthesis when their associated SEs were transcriptionally downregulated.
source: To investigate whether the observed decrease in Oct4 occupancy and eRNA synthesis at Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers coincided with a decrease of target mRNA synthesis, we paired transcriptionally downregulated SEs with their nearest transcribed genes. About half of these genes were downregulated (62 enhancer–gene pairs), and we found that mRNA synthesis decreased already after 3 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SE-gene pairs shown in Figure 4G.

claim: mRNA synthesis of SE-nearest genes decreased already after 3 hr of DOX treatment for downregulated SE-gene pairs.
source: To investigate whether the observed decrease in Oct4 occupancy and eRNA synthesis at Oct4-bound transcribed enhancers coincided with a decrease of target mRNA synthesis, we paired transcriptionally downregulated SEs with their nearest transcribed genes. About half of these genes were downregulated (62 enhancer–gene pairs), and we found that mRNA synthesis decreased already after 3 hr of DOX treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SE-gene pairs shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Oct4 occupancy and the degree of eRNA synthesis changes at transcriptionally downregulated SEs may play a role in transcription.
source: In addition to the possibility that the target gene may not always be the nearest gene, we found significantly lower occupancy of Oct4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, left) as well as significantly lower decrease of eRNA synthesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A, right) in comparison to the affected SEs. This suggests that Oct4 occupancy and the degree of eRNA synthesis changes at transcriptionally downregulated SEs may play a role in transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of SEs with downregulated versus unchanged nearest genes shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Oct4 activates both enhancer transcription and mRNA synthesis from its target genes.
source: Overall, these results are consistent with a function of Oct4 in activating both enhancer transcription and mRNA synthesis from its target genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Oct4 depletion led to decreased eRNA synthesis and decreased mRNA synthesis of target genes.

claim: Chromatin accessibility changes started to occur after 6 hr of DOX treatment, with the most substantial changes happening before 12 hr.
source: PCA indicated that accessibility changes started to occur after 6 hr of DOX treatment, with the most substantial changes happening before 12 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only few enhancers were detected to have significantly altered chromatin accessibility at 6 hr of DOX treatment.
source: In contrast to mRNAs and eRNAs (Figures 2A and 4A), only few enhancers were detected to have significantly altered chromatin accessibility at 6 hr (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 15 hr of DOX treatment resulted in a significant decrease of chromatin accessibility at 726 enhancers.
source: 15 hr of DOX treatment resulted in a significant decrease of chromatin accessibility at 726 enhancers (adjusted p value <0.01) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by DESeq2 analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For enhancers with decreased chromatin accessibility, chromatin accessibility remained largely unchanged at 3 hr of DOX treatment.
source: The kinetic analysis showed that for these enhancers, chromatin accessibility remained largely unchanged at 3 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For the downregulated SE–gene pairs chromatin accessibility was unaffected at 3 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Moreover, for the downregulated SE–gene pairs chromatin accessibility was unaffected at 3 hr (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of SE-gene pairs shown in Figure 4G–I.

claim: Decreased Oct4 binding does not immediately lead to chromatin accessibility changes, which occur later into the time course when Oct4 levels had considerably dropped.
source: These results show that decreased Oct4 binding does not immediately lead to chromatin accessibility changes, which occur later into the time course when Oct4 levels had considerably dropped.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromatin accessibility remained largely unchanged at 3 hr while Oct4 binding and eRNA synthesis decreased.

claim: For Oct4-sensitive enhancers, depletion of Oct4 led to a decrease in eRNA synthesis and a reduction of chromatin accessibility, with downregulation of eRNA synthesis preceding the decrease in accessibility.
source: In both groups, Oct4 binding to chromatin decreased over the time course and was associated with a decrease in eRNA synthesis (Figure 5D, E). For the first group, depletion of Oct4 led to a decrease in eRNA synthesis and a reduction of chromatin accessibility, with downregulation of eRNA synthesis preceding the decrease in accessibility (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: For Oct4-insensitive enhancers, depletion of Oct4 led to a decrease in eRNA synthesis without changes in chromatin accessibility.
source: For the second group, depletion of Oct4 led to a decrease in eRNA synthesis without changes in chromatin accessibility (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Reduced Oct4 binding leads to a delayed loss of chromatin accessibility at Oct4-sensitive enhancers compared to an immediate change of transcriptional activity.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that reduced Oct4 binding leads to a delayed loss of chromatin accessibility at Oct4-sensitive enhancers compared to an immediate change of transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eRNA synthesis decreased before chromatin accessibility at Oct4-sensitive enhancers.

claim: 95% and 86% of Oct4-sensitive and -insensitive enhancers, respectively, overlapped with Sox2 peaks.
source: Oct4 and Sox2 colocalize in both enhancer groups, with 95% and 86% of Oct4-sensitive and -insensitive enhancers, respectively, overlapping with Sox2 peaks (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed ~1.5-fold enrichment of Oct4 occupancy compared to Oct4-insensitive enhancers.
source: In metagene plots, Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed ~1.5-fold enrichment of Oct4 occupancy compared to Oct4-insensitive enhancers (Figure 6A), whereas Sox2, Nanog, Klf4, and Esrrb were only slightly enriched if at all (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Oct4-sensitive enhancers displayed higher levels of H3K27ac, whereas H3K4me1 showed similar levels compared to Oct4-insensitive enhancers.
source: Oct4-sensitive enhancers also displayed higher levels of H3K27ac, whereas H3K4me1 showed similar levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Oct4-sensitive enhancers were enriched for stem cell population maintenance.
source: According to genomic region enrichment analysis (McLean et al., 2010), Oct4-sensitive enhancers were enriched for stem cell population maintenance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and Oct4-insensitive enhancers for neural differentiation and development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by GREAT analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Oct4-insensitive enhancers were enriched for neural differentiation and development.
source: According to genomic region enrichment analysis (McLean et al., 2010), Oct4-sensitive enhancers were enriched for stem cell population maintenance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) and Oct4-insensitive enhancers for neural differentiation and development (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by GREAT analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed a strong enrichment for both Oct4 and the SoxOct composite motifs.
source: Our results showed a strong enrichment for both Oct4 and the SoxOct composite motifs at Oct4-sensitive enhancers only (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Oct4 influences chromatin accessibility preferentially when the SoxOct composite motif is present in DNA.
source: These findings suggest that Oct4 influences chromatin accessibility preferentially when the SoxOct composite motif is present in DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed strong enrichment for the SoxOct composite motif.

claim: At Oct4-sensitive enhancers, Sox2 remained bound from 0 to 6 hr and started to decrease after 9 hr of DOX treatment.
source: At Oct4-sensitive enhancers, Sox2 remained bound from 0 to 6 hr and started to decrease after 9 hr of treatment (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6C, D.

claim: At Oct4-insensitive, -independent, and -unbound transcribed enhancers, Sox2 occupancy was stable over the entire time course of Oct4 depletion.
source: At Oct4-insensitive, -independent, and -unbound transcribed enhancers, Sox2 occupancy was stable over the entire time course (Figure 6C, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 6C, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed a strong loss of Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog at 24 hr of DOX treatment.
source: Moreover, we analyzed published Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog ChIP-seq data at 0 and 24 hr after DOX treatment (King and Klose, 2017). Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed a strong loss of all three TFs at 24 hr, whereas Sox2 occupancy was unchanged and Nanog occupancy increased at 24 hr at Oct4-insensitive enhancers and -independent enhancers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Sox2 occupancy was unchanged and Nanog occupancy increased at 24 hr at Oct4-insensitive enhancers and -independent enhancers.
source: Moreover, we analyzed published Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog ChIP-seq data at 0 and 24 hr after DOX treatment (King and Klose, 2017). Oct4-sensitive enhancers showed a strong loss of all three TFs at 24 hr, whereas Sox2 occupancy was unchanged and Nanog occupancy increased at 24 hr at Oct4-insensitive enhancers and -independent enhancers (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis of published ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: During Oct4 depletion Sox2 binding and chromatin accessibility change with similar kinetics at Oct4-bound enhancers.
source: Taken together, these findings reveal that during Oct4 depletion Sox2 binding and chromatin accessibility change with similar kinetics at Oct4-bound enhancers.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sox2 remained bound at Oct4-sensitive enhancers until 6 hr and decreased after 9 hr, similar to chromatin accessibility changes.

claim: Low levels of Oct4 may cooperate with Sox2 to temporarily retain enhancers accessible.
source: This can be explained by the proposed model that low levels of Oct4 are sufficient to retain chromatin accessible, thus leading to a loss of Sox2 binding only when Oct4 levels decreased to the point where chromatin accessibility can no longer be maintained. This befits the pioneer role of Oct4 in creating an open chromatin environment to support binding of other pluripotency factors (Friman et al., 2019; King and Klose, 2017). In addition, reduced levels of Oct4 may cooperate with Sox2 to temporarily retain enhancers accessible.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sox2 remained bound at Oct4-sensitive enhancers during the first 6 hr of DOX treatment when Oct4 levels were reduced but not depleted.

claim: Oct4 may inhibit Sox2 binding at normal levels in ESCs.
source: Furthermore, we found enhanced binding of Sox2 at Oct4-bound enhancers after 3 hr of DOX treatment. This suggests that Oct4 may inhibit Sox2 binding at normal levels in ESCs, and agrees with a study that has shown that overexpression of Oct4 decreases Sox2 binding (Biddle et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Sox2 levels slightly increased at 3 hr of DOX treatment and supported by citation to Biddle et al., 2019.

claim: TF footprinting analysis detected a significant enrichment for Klf footprints at the later stages of Oct4 recovery.
source: Our TF footprinting analysis detected a significant enrichment for Klf footprints at the later stages of Oct4 recovery.
evidence: This is supported by TOBIAS analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Oct4 creates an open chromatin environment to prepare for binding of Klf TFs to support further maturation of the pluripotency network during Oct4 recovery.
source: Taken together, this implies that Oct4 creates an open chromatin environment to prepare for binding of Klf TFs to support further maturation of the pluripotency network during Oct4 recovery.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Klf footprints were enriched at later stages of Oct4 recovery and supported by knowledge about Klf TFs' role in pluripotency.

claim: Full depletion of Oct4 leads to rapid downregulation of key pluripotency factors.
source: In a recent study, Oct4 protein was fully depleted within 2 hr using an auxin-inducible degron system (Bates et al., 2021). Using RNA-seq, the authors showed that full depletion of Oct4 leads to rapid downregulation of key pluripotency factors, consistent with our results (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bates et al., 2021 and comparison to results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The used ZHBTc4 cells were contaminated with mycoplasma.
source: Analysis of the TT-seq data revealed that the used ZHBTc4 cells were contaminated with mycoplasma (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by analysis described in Materials and methods.

claim: The ZHBTc4 cells exhibit normal growth patterns and morphology despite mycoplasma contamination.
source: However, this does not alter the conclusions described in this manuscript. First, the ZHBTc4 cells exhibit normal growth patterns and morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Oct4 has differential concentration-dependent activities in regulating enhancer transcription and chromatin accessibility in pluripotent stem cells.
source: In summary, we investigated the role of Oct4 in regulating chromatin accessibility and transcriptional activity in pluripotent cells using high-resolution time course data for Oct4 depletion and subsequent recovery. We discovered that Oct4 has differential concentration-dependent activities in regulating enhancer transcription and chromatin accessibility in pluripotent stem cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oct4 regulates chromatin accessibility very rapidly even at low concentrations, capable of increasing chromatin accessibility within hours of induction.
source: In contrast, Oct4 regulates chromatin accessibility very rapidly even at low concentrations, capable of increasing chromatin accessibility within hours of induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromatin accessibility increased rapidly during partial recovery when Oct4 levels were still low (Figure 8C).

claim: The vast majority of ESCs could regain pluripotency after 15 hr of DOX treatment.
source: The vast majority of ESCs could regain pluripotency after 15 hr of DOX treatment, fewer cells could recover after longer depletion of up to 48 hr, and none could recover after 72 hr.
evidence: This is supported by AP staining results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Fewer ESCs could recover pluripotency after longer depletion of up to 48 hr of DOX treatment.
source: The vast majority of ESCs could regain pluripotency after 15 hr of DOX treatment, fewer cells could recover after longer depletion of up to 48 hr, and none could recover after 72 hr.
evidence: This is supported by AP staining results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: No ESCs could recover pluripotency after 72 hr of DOX treatment.
source: The vast majority of ESCs could regain pluripotency after 15 hr of DOX treatment, fewer cells could recover after longer depletion of up to 48 hr, and none could recover after 72 hr.
evidence: This is supported by AP staining results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: At Oct4-sensitive enhancers, there was a strong increase of chromatin accessibility already after 4.5 hr of DOX washout when the Oct4 protein level was still only around 9%.
source: At Oct4-sensitive enhancers, we found a strong increase of chromatin accessibility already after 4.5 hr when the Oct4 protein level was still only around 9% and the recovery of chromatin accessibility was mostly completed after 9 hr (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 8C and western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The recovery of chromatin accessibility at Oct4-sensitive enhancers was mostly completed after 9 hr of DOX washout.
source: At Oct4-sensitive enhancers, we found a strong increase of chromatin accessibility already after 4.5 hr when the Oct4 protein level was still only around 9% and the recovery of chromatin accessibility was mostly completed after 9 hr (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A weak but significant upregulation of eRNA synthesis occurred at Oct4-sensitive enhancers during Oct4 recovery.
source: A weak but significant upregulation of eRNA synthesis occured at Oct4-sensitive enhancers (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by TT-seq analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: At Oct4-insensitive enhancers, chromatin accessibility, and eRNA synthesis increased only slightly during Oct4 recovery.
source: At Oct4-insensitive enhancers, chromatin accessibility, and eRNA synthesis increased only slightly during Oct4 recovery (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: At Oct4-independent and -unbound transcribed enhancers, chromatin accessibility and eRNA synthesis remained unchanged during Oct4 recovery.
source: At Oct4-independent and -unbound transcribed enhancers, chromatin accessibility and eRNA synthesis remained unchanged (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: At 15 hr of DOX treatment, SoxOct footprints were the most significantly depleted in ATAC-seq signal, followed by Oct alone footprints.
source: In line with our previous motif analysis (Figure 6B), at 15 hr of DOX treatment, SoxOct footprints were the most significantly depleted in ATAC-seq signal, followed by Oct alone footprints (Figure 8—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by TOBIAS analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1G.

claim: SoxOct and Oct footprints were the most significantly enriched after 4.5 hr of Oct4 recovery.
source: Consistently, SoxOct and Oct footprints were the most significantly enriched after 4.5 hr of recovery (Figure 8—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by TOBIAS analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1H.

claim: After 9 hr of Oct4 recovery, open chromatin was enriched with not just SoxOct and Oct footprints, but also Klf footprints.
source: Interestingly, later into the recovery process – after 9 hr of washout, open chromatin was enriched with not just SoxOct and Oct footprints, but also Klf footprints (Figure 8—figure supplement 1I), inferring the role of Klf TFs in re-establishing of pluripotency after Oct4 depletion.
evidence: This is supported by TOBIAS analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1I.

claim: mRNA synthesis of previously upregulated genes decreased only slightly during Oct4 recovery.
source: Whereas mRNA synthesis of previously upregulated genes decreased only slightly, previously downregulated genes showed an increase of mRNA synthesis during Oct4 recovery (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Previously downregulated genes showed an increase of mRNA synthesis during Oct4 recovery.
source: Whereas mRNA synthesis of previously upregulated genes decreased only slightly, previously downregulated genes showed an increase of mRNA synthesis during Oct4 recovery (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: For most of the SE-controlled downregulated genes, an increase in mRNA synthesis was observed during Oct4 recovery.
source: In particular, for most of the SE-controlled downregulated genes (Figures 2H and 4G), we observed an increase in mRNA synthesis (Figure 8F), accompanied by an increase in chromatin accessibility and eRNA synthesis at their paired enhancers (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Increase in mRNA synthesis of SE-controlled downregulated genes during Oct4 recovery was accompanied by an increase in chromatin accessibility and eRNA synthesis at their paired enhancers.
source: In particular, for most of the SE-controlled downregulated genes (Figures 2H and 4G), we observed an increase in mRNA synthesis (Figure 8F), accompanied by an increase in chromatin accessibility and eRNA synthesis at their paired enhancers (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Partial recovery of Oct4 rapidly increases chromatin accessibility, followed by rebound of gene transcription activity, with the recovery of associated enhancer transcription being weaker.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that partial recovery of Oct4 rapidly increases chromatin accessibility, followed by rebound of gene transcription activity, with the recovery of associated enhancer transcription being weaker.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that chromatin accessibility recovered rapidly and strongly, while eRNA synthesis showed only weak recovery during partial Oct4 recovery.

claim: Loss of Oct4 from enhancers goes along with a decrease in mRNA synthesis from Oct4 target genes crucial for maintaining pluripotency.
source: Our data showed that loss of Oct4 from enhancers goes along with a decrease in mRNA synthesis from Oct4 target genes crucial for maintaining pluripotency.
evidence: This is supported by TT-seq and ChIP-seq data showing coordinated decrease of Oct4 binding and mRNA synthesis of pluripotency genes.

claim: During Oct4 depletion, enhancer and target gene transcription were very sensitive to even small reductions of Oct4 binding.
source: During Oct4 depletion, enhancer and target gene transcription were very sensitive to even small reductions of Oct4 binding, whereas chromatin accessibility was either unaffected (Oct4-insensitive enhancers) or affected later when Oct4 levels decreased considerably (Oct4-sensitive enhancers).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eRNA and mRNA synthesis decreased after 3 hr while chromatin accessibility remained largely unchanged.

claim: During partial recovery of Oct4, chromatin accessibility and enhancer transcription increased at Oct4-sensitive enhancers, but eRNA synthesis could not be fully reactivated, although chromatin accessibility was largely restored.
source: During partial recovery of Oct4, chromatin accessibility and enhancer transcription increased at Oct4-sensitive enhancers, but eRNA synthesis could not be fully reactivated, although chromatin accessibility was largely restored.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and TT-seq data during Oct4 recovery showing strong recovery of chromatin accessibility but weak recovery of eRNA synthesis.

claim: Oct4 is thought to activate pluripotency genes by forming phase-separated condensates at SEs.
source: Oct4 is thought to activate pluripotency genes by forming phase-separated condensates at SEs (Boija et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boija et al., 2018.

claim: High levels of Oct4 are required to maintain and reactivate transcription.
source: This model is consistent with our observation that high levels of Oct4 are required to maintain and reactivate transcription in recovery experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that eRNA synthesis decreased rapidly during depletion and could not be fully recovered during partial recovery.

claim: ESCs with reduced Oct4 expression maintained a robust naive pluripotent state, but only wild-type Oct4 levels could enable effective differentiation to all embryonic lineages.
source: As shown previously, ESCs with reduced Oct4 expression maintained a robust naive pluripotent state, but only wild-type Oct4 levels could enable effective differentiation to all embryonic lineages (Karwacki-Neisius et al., 2013; Radzisheuskaya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karwacki-Neisius et al., 2013 and Radzisheuskaya et al., 2013.
